intro: Crawford County, county seat Grayling, sits on the southern and eastern edge of the Antrim Shale trend, more of a flank position than the dense core drilling you'd find in Otsego or Antrim County. That doesn't mean nothing was drilled here, it means the well spacing and production history look a little different, and a mineral interest in Crawford County needs to be checked against its own specific section rather than assumed to match what a neighboring county's wells did.

Grayling itself grew up around the railroad and the timber industry before Camp Grayling and the Au Sable River recreation economy took over as the county's identity. A lot of the private land around town and out toward Frederic and Lovells carries mineral ownership that split off from the surface generations ago, often tied to old logging-era land patents, and a fair number of owners we talk to in this county have no idea whether their interest was ever leased, let alone drilled.

sections.heading: Flank position versus core, and why it matters
paragraphs: Being on the flank of the Antrim trend rather than dead center means well density in Crawford County is lower than in the core counties to the north. Some sections here got drilled during the Section 29 tax-credit boom of the late 1980s and 1990s, others never saw a rig even though a lease got signed. If your family's mineral interest is tied to land that was leased but never drilled, that lease may well have expired decades ago, which changes the picture entirely from an interest tied to a producing well.

The Antrim Shale itself is biogenic gas, shallow, and slow to develop without dewatering, and where it was drilled in this county the wells behave the same way they do further north, a long flat decline rather than a sharp drop-off. But you can't assume your parcel was part of that activity just because the county name shows up on an Antrim map. We check section-specific records before saying anything about your interest.

sections.heading: Ownership tied to old timber and homestead land
paragraphs: Crawford County's land history runs heavy through the logging era, when huge tracts changed hands fast and cheap after the original timber was cut. Mineral rights on a lot of that ground got separated from the surface during those transactions or in the decades after, sometimes reserved by a timber company, sometimes sold off individually to speculators who leased them out during later oil and gas booms.

That layered history means Crawford County title can be genuinely messy, multiple owners, missing links in the chain, interests that were never recorded clearly. The Crawford County register of deeds in Grayling holds what documentation exists, and pulling that chain is usually the first real step before we can put a number on anything.

sections.heading: What we look at before quoting a Crawford County interest
paragraphs: Because this county sits on the flank rather than the core, the first question we answer is whether your interest is tied to an actual producing well or to acreage that was only ever leased. If there's production, we check current volumes and recent royalty statements against the well's history and remaining reserve life. If there's no production, the interest may still have some value for future leasing potential, but it's a very different, more speculative conversation than a producing royalty interest.
We won't quote a flat per-acre number for Crawford County without knowing which situation you're in, and you should be skeptical of anyone who does.

sections.heading: Sorting out title before a sale
paragraphs: Given how much Crawford County mineral ownership traces back to old timber-era land splits, we frequently work with owners who aren't fully sure what they hold. That's a normal starting point. Bring whatever deed, probate, or old lease paperwork you have, even if it looks incomplete, and we'll help figure out what's actually there before talking numbers.

faqs.question: Is Crawford County part of the Antrim Shale play?
faqs.answer: It sits on the southern flank of the trend, so some sections saw drilling during the Antrim boom and others didn't. It's not automatically core acreage the way Otsego or Antrim County is, so we check your specific section before saying much about production potential.

faqs.question: My family has an old lease from the 1980s on Crawford County land that was never drilled. Does it still mean anything?
faqs.answer: Most oil and gas leases have primary terms of a few years and expire if no well is drilled and no production established within that window, unless there's language extending it. An old undrilled lease from the 1980s has very likely expired, which means your mineral rights are unencumbered, which is worth knowing either way.

faqs.question: How do I find out if my Crawford County land has ever been leased or drilled?
faqs.answer: Start at the Crawford County register of deeds in Grayling to check for recorded leases against your parcel, and the state's oil and gas well records can confirm whether a well was ever permitted or drilled nearby.

faqs.question: Is a non-producing mineral interest in Crawford County worth anything?
faqs.answer: It can have some value tied to future leasing potential, but it's more speculative than a producing royalty interest with an income history behind it. We'll be straight with you about which category your interest falls into before discussing numbers.

faqs.question: What documents do you need to evaluate my Crawford County mineral rights?
faqs.answer: A deed or probate document showing your ownership, any lease paperwork if you have it, and a royalty statement or division order if the interest has ever produced. Even partial records are a useful starting point.
